claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element alloy with its constituent metals in nearly equiatomic ratios.
Nitrogen-atmosphere thermal annealing followed by acid etching will form a Pt-enriched surface layer.
The proposed treatment will incorporate nitrogen into the near-surface region.
Nitrogen doping produces robust metal–nitrogen bonds that stabilize the catalyst.
Stable M–N bonds, particularly Ni–N and Co–N bonds, suppress dissolution or oxidation of less noble transition metals.
The Pt-rich shell itself minimizes dissolution and degradation of the base metals.
Nitrogen incorporation modifies the electronic structure of surface Pt.
The Pt-rich high-entropy surface and nitrogen doping regulate the binding energies of intermediates such as *O and *OH.
The modified surface reduces catalyst poisoning.
Nitrogen doping and M–N bonding enhance corrosion resistance and inhibit dissolution of the Pt shell.
The combined Pt-rich shell and nitrogen-doped structure will maintain high activity and durability under harsh, fluctuating automotive exhaust conditions.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the modification will reduce activity loss and improve durability during transient, low-temperature operation with H2O and NO exposure and aging.
A Pt-rich surface permits low overall Pt usage through efficient use of surface Pt.
The untreated nearly equiatomic catalyst suffers activity degradation under transient gasoline or hybrid-vehicle exhaust conditions.
The modification should be particularly effective under low-temperature transient exhaust conditions containing H2O and NO.
The benefit may be lost if thermal or chemical stresses exceed the stability range of the Pt-rich, nitrogen-doped layer.
The optimal nitrogen-doping level and Pt-shell thickness have not been determined.
The magnitude of improvement under automotive exhaust conditions remains uncertain until directly tested.
An otherwise equivalent treatment performed without nitrogen will yield a control lacking nitrogen doping.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in sustained activity, durability, and Pt retention relative to untreated and nitrogen-free controls would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The design specifies only two batches—the full treatment and a nitrogen-free treated control—but the falsification rule also requires comparison with an untreated control that is not included in the stated preparation design.
